title: Words at work
grammar: Word formation for B2 (noun/adjective/adverb suffixes, negative prefixes)

scene.speaker: nova
scene.bubble: Words don't just sit still — they grow into whole families! Meet the words that build a career, and get ready for the multiple matching task.
scene.intro: Welcome to Unit 3. Our Trades project turns to the language of the workplace itself — apprenticeships, motivation, teamwork and the everyday words that describe a job well done. In this unit you read how four B2 students describe their first taste of work, in the format of Reading Part 7, learn the suffixes and prefixes that build noun, adjective and adverb families, meet the compound adjectives that describe a job (well-paid, hard-working, rewarding), and listen to a real interview about a trade. By the end you will be ready for the word-formation task and for describing your own dream job. Let's get to work.

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 1 and 2. Talk with a partner, then record yourself.

tips.expect: Part 1 (about 2 minutes): the examiner asks you and your partner questions about yourselves — work, study and future plans. Part 2 (about 3 minutes): each of you talks alone for about a minute about two of three photographs, answering a printed question; then your partner answers a short question about your photographs in about 20 seconds.
how: In Part 2, do not describe every detail of the photographs. Choose two of the three, compare them directly (In the first picture… whereas in the second…) and answer both parts of the question.
Keep talking for the whole minute — if you run out of ideas, speculate about how the people might be feeling.
In Part 1, answer with a reason or an example, not a single word.
tips.remember: You only need to talk about two of the three photographs, and the examiner is listening for language, not for a 'correct' opinion.

data.text: Part 1: talk about jobs and work experience. Part 2: compare two of the photographs and say why the people might have chosen these jobs.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 7 — multiple matching. Read about four students' first jobs and match the questions to the person.

tips.expect: One text divided into several short sections, usually different people talking about a related experience, followed by ten questions. Each question matches one section; a section can match more than one question.
how: Read the ten questions first and underline the key idea of each one.
Read each section and note, in one word, what it is mainly about — then check it against the questions.
The questions paraphrase the text closely: look for a different way of saying the same idea, not the same words repeated.
tips.remember: Do not assume the answers follow the order of the sections — work through the text in order and tick off questions as you find them.

data.title: My first taste of work
data.intro:
As part of Inspiring Nordic, five B2 and 11 students describe the first job or apprenticeship that taught them something about the world of work.

For questions 1–10, choose from the people (A–E). The people may be chosen more than once.

sections.heading: Sofía
sections.text: I got my first job last summer, at a small bakery two streets from my house. I remember being nervous on my very first morning — I had never worked with the public before, and I was worried I would make a mess of the till. The owner, Mrs Lund, paired me with an older colleague called Erik, and within a week we had become a proper team. He taught me how to organise the shelves and how to talk to customers who were in a hurry. By the end of the summer I had discovered something surprising: I actually enjoyed being given responsibility, from opening the shop to counting the money at closing time. It made me feel useful in a way that school rarely does.

sections.heading: Mateo
sections.text: My uncle is an electrician, and last winter he let me help him on small jobs at weekends. Everything I know, I learned directly from him — how to read a wiring plan, how to stay safe around a live circuit, and, above all, patience. At first I found the work repetitive, but then he let me finish a job on my own, under his eyes, and something clicked. Now I am saving every spare pound so that I can enrol on a proper electrical course next year and finally get an official qualification. My uncle says that a good tradesperson never stops learning, and I believe him completely — every visit teaches me something new about the trade.

sections.heading: Liam
sections.text: For two summers I have worked as a lifeguard at our local pool, and it is nothing like I expected. The early starts were hard at first, but the real challenge is staying completely calm if something goes wrong, because panicking helps nobody. My colleagues and I check the water constantly, and we trust each other completely — one whistle from anyone and we all react at once. Once I actually had to pull a young boy out of the deep end, and afterwards my hands were shaking, though my voice stayed steady the whole time. With the money I earned I finally bought the racing bike I had wanted for two years, which felt like the perfect reward.

sections.heading: Nadia
sections.text: I never planned to get a job at the animal shelter; I started by volunteering there on Saturdays because I love dogs. After a few months the manager noticed how reliable I had become and offered me a few paid hours during the week, feeding the animals and cleaning their cages. It is not glamorous work, but caring for a frightened rescue dog and watching it relax is genuinely rewarding. Through the shelter I met a vet who let me watch her examine the animals, and now I am seriously considering training in animal care once I finish school — something I would never have imagined a year ago.

sections.heading: Astrid
sections.text: Last summer I did a two-month apprenticeship at my grandfather's old boatyard, learning how traditional wooden boats are repaired. Nobody warned me how physically demanding it would be: by the first evening my arms ached from sanding and lifting, and I nearly gave up. My mentor, an elderly craftsman named Sven, never raised his voice, even when I made mistakes, and slowly I began to understand the pride he takes in his work. He earns far less than my cousin who works in an office, yet he is clearly the happier of the two. That summer taught me that a well-paid job is not automatically the most satisfying one.

activities.title: Language focus 1 — word formation: suffixes and prefixes

data.title: Word formation for B2: suffixes and prefixes
data.can: I can change a root word into the noun, adjective, adverb or negative form that a sentence needs, using the suffixes and prefixes tested in Part 3.
data.intro: In the word-formation task you are given a root word in capitals and you must change its form — often its word class — so that it fits the gap naturally. Recognising the common suffixes and prefixes below will help you do this quickly and confidently.

examples.text: They admired his kindness towards new staff.
Many apprentices feel disorganised in their first week.

rules: Noun suffixes: -ment, -tion, -ness, -ity, -ship (commit→commitment, motivate→motivation, kind→kindness, reliable→reliability, apprentice→apprenticeship).
Adjective suffixes: -ful, -less, -ous, -al, -ive (resource→resourceful, care→careless, ambition→ambitious, profession→professional, create→creative).
Adverb suffix: -ly is added to the adjective, not the root (confident→confidently, professional→professionally).

Negative prefixes un-, in-, dis-, im- reverse the meaning: employ→unemployed, formal→informal, organise→disorganise, possible→impossible. There is no fixed rule for which prefix a word takes — learn them with the word.
Read the whole sentence before you decide: is the missing word positive or negative? singular or plural? a person (-er/-or) or a quality (-ness/-ity)?

practice.instructions: Choose the correct form of the word in capitals.

items.sentence: My cousin has a ___ job in finance, but he never has time for his hobbies. (PAY well)
Her ___ is obvious in everything she does. (MOTIVATE)
He always gives a ___ answer to difficult questions, even under pressure. (RESOURCE)
Sadly, local ___ has risen again this year. (EMPLOY)
She spoke very ___ during the interview for the apprenticeship. (PROFESSION)

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 3 — word formation. Use the word in capitals to form a word that fits each gap.

tips.expect: A short text with eight gaps. Each gap has a root word in capitals beside it; you must change its form — often into a different word class — to complete the sentence correctly.
how: Decide first what part of speech the gap needs: a noun, an adjective, an adverb, or perhaps a negative form.
Check for a plural, a negative prefix, or a change of spelling before you commit to an answer.
Once you've written your answer, read the whole sentence again — does it make sense and sound natural?
tips.remember: The base word almost never fits the gap unchanged — if your answer is identical to the word in capitals, look again.

data.title: Learning a trade the Nordic way
data.text: Across the region, an increasing number of teenagers are choosing an {1:APPRENTICE} instead of going straight to university, and the change is easy to notice in every local workshop. The shift reflects growing {2:MOTIVATE} among young people who want practical, hands-on skills rather than another three years in a classroom. Local employers say that {3:RELY} workers are hard to find, so many are happy to train teenagers themselves rather than wait for the perfect finished candidate to apply. According to one carpenter who has taken on apprentices for a decade, the {4:RESPONSIBLE} of guiding a new apprentice is genuinely {5:REWARD}, even when it slows the job down and tests his patience. Schools, too, have become far more {6:PROFESSION} about the process lately, offering proper careers advice and organising visits to local workshops so that students can see a trade close up before choosing it. Critics once thought that manual trades were {7:USE} for ambitious students, something to fall back on rather than aim for, but that old opinion is now {8:DOUBT} out of date. Employers, teachers and students all seem to agree: learning a trade properly builds confidence as fast as any exam does.

activities.title: Listening Part 4 — multiple choice. Listen to the interview and choose the best answer.

tips.expect: A single interview or conversation of about four minutes, with seven four-option questions testing opinion, attitude, detail and general meaning. You hear it twice.
how: Before listening, read all seven questions and options — they follow the order of the interview.
Listen for the speaker's opinion or feeling, not just facts: a change of tone or a phrase like 'to be honest' often signals the answer.
On the second listening, check any answers you were unsure of and eliminate options that are only partly true.
tips.remember: Wrong options are often mentioned in the recording but twisted slightly — choose what the speaker really means, not just what you recognise.

data.voice_note: Presenter (Ryan) interviews Sven, a boat-builder, about his trade and his apprenticeship.
data.script:
Presenter: Welcome back to Career Talk, the programme where we meet people who love their trade. Today I'm speaking to Sven, who has been building traditional wooden boats for over twenty years. Sven, thanks for joining us.
Sven: It's a pleasure to be here, Ryan.
Presenter: Let's start at the beginning. How did you actually get into boat-building?
Sven: Almost by accident, to be honest. I left school without much idea of what I wanted to do, and a neighbour who ran a small boatyard offered me a few weeks of work over the summer. I only meant to stay until September, but I never really left. Twenty-two years later, here I still am.
Presenter: What was your apprenticeship actually like?
Sven: Hard, in the best sense. My first jobs were sanding, sweeping and carrying wood — nothing glamorous at all. The owner, old Lars, barely explained anything; he expected me to watch closely and ask questions only when I was truly stuck. It frustrated me at first, but I now think it was the right approach, because I learned to notice details for myself instead of waiting to be told.
Presenter: Many people assume a trade like yours is badly paid. Is that fair?
Sven: It's true that I earn less than friends who went into finance or law, and I won't pretend that never bothers me. But I measure the job differently. When a family sails away in a boat I repaired with my own hands, that feeling is worth more to me than a bigger salary would be. Money isn't nothing, but it isn't everything either.
Presenter: What do you enjoy least about the work?
Sven: The waiting, honestly. Wood needs time — glue needs time to set, paint needs time to dry — and in a world that wants everything instantly, that patience is hard for some young apprentices to accept. I still have to remind myself, after all these years, that rushing a boat never actually saves time in the end; it just creates a boat that leaks.
Presenter: What advice would you give a teenager considering an apprenticeship like yours?
Sven: Don't choose it because you dislike school; choose it because you genuinely want to build something with your hands. And find a workshop where the older workers are willing to teach, not just to give orders — that difference matters more than people realise. A good mentor can turn a difficult first year into an enjoyable one.
Presenter: Finally, what keeps you motivated after two decades in the same boatyard?
Sven: Every boat is slightly different, so I'm never doing exactly the same job twice. And, honestly, there's something quietly satisfying about a trade that will still matter in a hundred years, long after most of today's fashionable jobs have disappeared.
Presenter: Sven, thank you very much for your time.
Sven: Thank you, Ryan. It's been a pleasure.

activities.title: Language focus 2 — compound adjectives and -ing/-ed adjectives

data.title: Compound adjectives and -ing/-ed adjectives for describing jobs
data.can: I can build compound adjectives like well-paid and hard-working, and choose correctly between an -ing and an -ed adjective.
data.intro: English often describes a job or a worker by joining two words together with a hyphen, or by using the -ing/-ed forms of a verb as adjectives. Getting these right makes your speaking and writing sound much more natural.

examples.text: She finally found a well-paid job in the city.
It isn't a badly-paid job, but it's exhausting.
Many apprentices find the first year rewarding.
examples.note: -ing adjective: the job causes the feeling

examples.text: By the end of the day the apprentices felt rewarded.
examples.note: -ed adjective: the person feels the result

examples.text: A genuinely fulfilling career doesn't have to be well-paid.
After the long shift, Sven looked completely exhausted.

rules: Compound adjectives often follow the pattern adverb/noun + past participle: well-paid, badly-paid, hand-made, self-employed. They go before the noun and never change form.
Compound adjectives can also be adjective/noun + present participle: hard-working, good-looking, easy-going.
-ing adjectives describe what causes a feeling (a rewarding job, a motivating boss); -ed adjectives describe the person who feels it (a motivated apprentice, an exhausted worker).
Do not confuse the two: 'I am boring' means you cause boredom in others; 'I am bored' means you feel it.
Hyphenate compound adjectives before a noun (a well-paid job); many are also used after 'be' without changing (the job is well-paid).

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations

tips.expect: Six separate sentences. For each, you complete a second sentence with the same meaning as the first, using a given key word that must not be changed. You write between two and five words, including the key word. Each item is worth up to two marks.
how: Identify the structure being tested — often a fixed phrase, a comparative, a passive, or a verb pattern.
Write the whole gap first, then read the complete sentence: does it mean exactly the same as the first sentence?
Count your words carefully, including the key word — going over five words scores nothing, even if the grammar is correct.
tips.remember: You can often score half marks: getting the main structure right, even with a small error, is better than leaving the gap empty.

activities.title: Writing Part 2 — article. Plan, write 140–190 words and hand it in.

tips.expect: Part 2 offers a choice of task types — often an article, an email, a review or a story. For an article you usually respond to a question for a magazine read by other students, using an engaging opening and a personal, friendly tone. 140–190 words, neutral to informal register.
how: Grab the reader's attention in your opening line — a question, a surprising statement, or a mini scene works well.
Organise your ideas in short paragraphs, each with one clear idea.
Address the reader directly sometimes (you might think…, imagine…) — that's what makes an article different from an essay.
tips.remember: An article is read for interest, not just information — a flat list of facts without any personal voice loses marks for communicative achievement.

data.task:
You see this announcement on your school's website.

Articles wanted for the school magazine!

The job I'd love to do

Tell us about a job you would love to do one day. What does the job involve? Why does it appeal to you, and what skills or qualifications would you need?

The best articles will be published in our next issue.

Write your article.
plan: Opening (1–2 sentences): grab attention — a question or a short scene, then name the job.
Paragraph 2: what the job involves, in your own words, and why it appeals to you personally.
Paragraph 3: the skills, qualities or qualifications the job would need, using at least one word-formation item from this unit.
Closing: a short, memorable final thought — not a formal conclusion.

Grabbing attention: Have you ever wondered what it's like to…?
Ever since I was little, I've dreamt of…
Explaining appeal: What appeals to me most is…
Unlike most jobs, this one would let me…
Talking about skills: You would need to be genuinely…
Closing: So watch this space — one day that could be me.
Who knows? Maybe I'll see you there.
One thing's for sure: I won't be choosing a boring job.

checklist: My opening line would make someone want to keep reading.
I named the job early and explained why it appeals to me.
I mentioned real skills or qualifications, using at least one word-formation word.
My tone is personal and friendly, suitable for a school magazine.
I organised my ideas into clear short paragraphs with a strong closing line.
data.model:
A model answer (146 words). Notice the engaging opening, the personal tone and the short, magazine-style paragraphs.

Ever since I watched a documentary about wildlife photographers, I've dreamt of one job: travelling the world with a camera, capturing animals that most people will never see in real life.

What appeals to me most is the mixture of patience and adventure. You might wait three days in the rain for one perfect shot of a fox, then fly somewhere completely different the following week. It's never, ever boring.

Of course, it isn't an easy career to fall into. You would need real technical expertise with cameras and editing software, and a qualification in biology or environmental science definitely helps. More than anything, though, you need to be hard-working and endlessly patient — nature doesn't perform on command.

Will I actually manage it? I honestly don't know. But every time I pick up a camera, it feels like the right direction to be heading in.

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 3 and 4. Collaborative task and discussion. Record your best answer.

tips.expect: Part 3 (about 4 minutes): you and your partner discuss a question using five written prompts for about two minutes, then take one minute to reach a decision together. Part 4 (about 4 minutes): the examiner asks you both broader questions on the same topic.
how: In Part 3 you are marked on how you interact, not on whether you agree — ask your partner's opinion and respond to it.
You don't have to discuss all five prompts. Two or three, explored properly, are better than five rushed ones.
In the decision minute, negotiate rather than simply agreeing: give a reason for your final choice.
In Part 4, extend your answers with a reason and an example — don't just answer yes or no.
tips.remember: Look at your partner during Part 3, not at the examiner — the examiner is assessing your conversation, not judging your opinions.
